cards.title: Masumi Yamada
cards.sub: 2015 · Disaster Prevention Research Institute, Kyoto University
cards.prompt: The 2011 false alarms could not be fixed by waiting longer or by adding stations. Yamada and three co-authors changed one step of the pipeline instead. Which step, and what does the need for that step tell you about what a P-wave pick does not carry?
cards.answer: The association step: deciding which earthquake each pick belongs to. They made it probabilistic, treating the number of concurrent earthquakes as something to infer rather than assume, and fed it maximum displacement amplitude alongside picking times. A pick carries no label naming its source, so completeness is a fact about each source, not about the stream they share.
cards.body: Masumi Yamada, at Kyoto University's Disaster Prevention Research Institute. With S. Wu and J. L. Beck at Caltech and Koji Tamaribuchi at JMA, she worked the 2011 aftershock sequence backwards. The picks were real arrivals, correctly timed. What had failed was the step that decides which earthquake each one belongs to.

cards.title: The two months after Tohoku
cards.prompt: In the two months after the main shock, JMA's public warnings were wrong more often than they were right. How many of the 70 were inappropriate, and what share of those came from the concurrent-event problem rather than from broken sensors?
cards.answer: 44 of the 70 were inappropriate, misses and false alarms counted together. Over 70 per cent of the 44 were caused by multiple concurrent events.
cards.body: Japan's early warning system had just done the thing it was built for: an early warning on 11 March, before the S-wave reached anywhere in the country. Then the aftershock sequence began, several earthquakes at a time, and warnings went out for shaking that never came, while some that mattered never went out at all.

cards.title: Wu, Yamada, Tamaribuchi and Beck
cards.prompt: This paper states, in one sentence, how two earthquakes become one inside the JMA pipeline. Reproduce it using the terms 'near source' and 'far source', name the quantity it corrupts, and say why holding the window open longer would have made the error worse rather than better.
cards.answer: Some of the near source stations of the second event were treated as far source stations of the first. Distance is inferred from arrival time, so a strong nearby reading is priced as a weak distant one; that corrupts the magnitude upward, which is why the result is a false alarm. Extra waiting only admits more of the second event's arrivals into the first event's estimate, so slack feeds the error instead of curing it.
cards.body: 'Multi-events earthquake early warning algorithm using a Bayesian approach', doi 10.1093/gji/ggu437, online 11 December 2014. Eighteen pages of Bayesian model selection whose first question is not where the earthquake is but how many earthquakes there are. Tamaribuchi is at JMA, so the operator co-authored the count of its own failures.

cards.title: IPF, and the January that repeated it
cards.prompt: JMA shipped the multi-event associator and hit the same wall fourteen months later. What did the January 2018 pair do that IPF was built to prevent, which part of the pipeline was actually at fault, and what does that leave you owing at the whiteboard?
cards.answer: Two earthquakes about 400 km apart broke at the same time; the M4.5's magnitude was calculated with the M4.0's displacement amplitudes and the predicted shaking came out at least two intensity units high. IPF and NYAD located both events correctly - the event identification step after them associated the two wrongly. A smarter cutoff narrows the failure, it never removes it, so anything that closes a window early also owes a way to correct the number afterwards.
cards.body: IPF entered JMA operation on 14 December 2016, weighing amplitude as well as travel-time difference before it associates a pick. PLUM followed on 22 March 2018, predicting shaking directly from ground motion observed near the target instead of from a source estimate. 150 S-net ocean-bottom seismometers were added in 2019 and 2020.
